source.title: Generalization at the Edge of Stability
source.authors: M. Tuci; Caner Korkmaz; Umut Simsekli; Tolga Birdal

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates training and test accuracy during grokking on modular addition, using its own experimental setup. It does not reproduce the original study’s full set of dataset-size comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports grokking experiments on modular addition and explicitly states that training accuracy reaches 100% early while test accuracy continues to rise. It does not report a sweep over training-set sizes or state that test accuracy begins at chance. Correlations between sharpness-dimension measures and generalization gaps are not rows for the circuit-formation claims because the study does not analyze the generalizing circuit or its formation.
record.test_reason: The study uses grokking on modular addition (mod 97, fixed 40/60 split) as a testbed for its own Sharpness Dimension measure. Its stated aim is to 'induce and observe grokking', with hyperparameters chosen for that purpose. It then reports only how well SD and other complexity measures correlate with the generalization gap. Train and test accuracy are given only qualitatively, as confirmation that grokking occurred. There is no dataset-size sweep, no stated chance-level start and no comparison with non-grokking runs, so its results do not bear on whether V1 holds. The Hessian-based measure is not a circuit-formation progress measure (V2). Weight decay is present but not varied against dataset size (V5).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the Sharpness Dimension, a Lyapunov-inspired measure of the full Hessian spectrum, bounds and empirically predicts generalization gaps at the edge of stability. They also find it correlates with grokking phase transitions. They make no claim about grokking's mechanism, its dependence on dataset size, or its circuits.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular addition and training/test accuracy to study delayed generalization, but uses the paper’s own network, optimizer, and fixed 40%/60% split; it does not report a training-set-size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The grokking experiments vary learning rate, weight decay, seed, and, in the appendix, architecture; individual main-figure parameter assignments are not stated in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: In the grokking runs, the Sharpness Dimension correlates with the generalization gap across 100 checkpoints (Fig. 4). In one 3-layer MLP run, SD rises while test accuracy climbs slowly, drops sharply during the sharp rise, then rises again. The other measures (trace, sharpness, E_alpha) decrease monotonically.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A Hessian-spectrum complexity measure (Sharpness Dimension) changes non-monotonically in step with the grokking phase transition and tracks the generalization gap.

record.problems: The grokking evaluation uses a fixed 40%/60% split, so it cannot establish how delay changes with training-set size. Accuracy values and the initial test accuracy are not stated; some outcomes are shown only in figures.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size; start of test accuracy at chance; the jump size relative to non-grokking controls.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V1 'supports' label is downgraded. The grokking experiment is a deliberately induced testbed for the authors' own metric. The accuracy descriptions are qualitative confirmations that grokking occurred, not measured tests of V1, so no verdicts are given. The GPT-2 and MNIST experiments concern generalization-gap correlations, not delayed generalization, and do not bear on V3 or V4. The Fig. 4 caption labels both rows as '2-layer MLP', apparently a typo.

versions.untested_parts: The effect of training-set size on the delay is not tested. The text does not establish that test accuracy starts at chance.
